The story effectively captures a range of distinct perspectives, including those of a thirteen-year-old girl navigating adolescence and impending grief, her cynical yet fiercely loving dying father, a community of gay men in the late 1990s celebrating life amidst the shadow of the AIDS crisis, and a pragmatic fifteen-year-old Mexican crew member (Mateo) who views the cruise and the illness through a working-class, matter-of-fact lens. 

Furthermore, the story features an unappealing character in Clara's mother, Deborah. Though her appearance is brief, her perspective—rooted in upper-middle-class suburban propriety, latent homophobia, and a desire to sanitize uncomfortable realities (such as instructing Clara to call her father's AIDS "an autoimmune condition similar to lupus")—is presented with convincing accuracy. Rather than making her a cartoon villain, the writer grounds her objections in believable parental anxiety and suburban conformity, which effectively contrasts with the vibrant, authentic community on the ship.
